chapter: Freelancing, Miller and the girls' bands
title: Politicians, racketeers and segregation trouble at the pier
summary: Wires were cut on the pier, and his plan for a night for whites drew complaints of segregating from black musicians.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Who was booking you in those days then?
Ah, I was going to say, since you did well, if you'd got a booker they would have continued, wouldn't they?

Yeah, well, it hurt them so bad until they started to -- I was playing out on the pier, too. Came there one night and all the wires was cut. So I went to the D.A. and he made them give me some light on Sunday. And hook up to anything.

So I'll say this, the politicians was on me on one hand and the racketeers on the other. Politicians was trying to hold me there, but the racket men (inaudible). So I made a deal with the city by Pleasure Beach. If they wanted me to

the whites on a Sunday, see, because we lost so much money over here, with Harry James tonight and you over there. They said, you'd got to the whites. So I put up a sign I was going to the whites, and all the black musicians come down on me right away for segregating.

And I couldn't get out of that, and I went back and said you can't do that no more. I said, the whites -- and so, I said, well, I'll put up a sign, special party tonight, and I tried it that way and that wouldn't work. And those white kids was coming from New Haven and they wasn't going to play the (unintelligible). You can imagine what those guys -- the same (unintelligible). Ben Smith was in the band, then, too.
And he wrote that song, (unintelligible). And people could tell when you really had it, when you was really putting it down.
